I am an accomplished ultra-runner. It's great to see folks getting into running, but these C25K programs confuse me. Don't take my comments as any type of criticism, I'd just like to get more info. Are you overweight/obese? How many days a week do you run? Are you under 50 years old (and can you give me a ballpark of your age)?

If you're not significantly overweight and relatively young there is no reason why you shouldn't be jogging 5 days a week. Speed is not the primary thing you should be focused on--be cognizant and mindful of your FORM. Watch this video on form--it is spot on. Constantly monitor yourself during your run as to your form. Take mental notes. The longer you jog the more your form degrades--that's why you take the mental notes--so you can notice and correct problems--"hey, I'm not picking my knees up like I should be" or "I'm looking at the ground a lot--I should be keeping my chin up and looking at the horizon."

I trust you purchased some REAL running shoes recently and are not just using some all-purpose sneakers. Real running shoes can be found cheaply online. Running in the wrong or worn out shoes will destroy your body.

I run one day a week to mix in with my hybrid workout program. I have gone all the way through p90x and p90x3. I am 6 feet and 205lbs I wear a size 36 and it is loose. I am older than 20 and younger than 40.

I do this to get cardio and build endurance.

Just a couple of thoughts. First off, running one day a week isn't good at all. The reason is that you're not actually building anything that way. I assume you've got a cardio baseline from P90X, but jogging/running requires a shit-ton of stabilization muscles, core, etc. If you try to "improve" every week, you'll most certainly end up getting an injury. If you want to improve your running, then--at an absolute minimum--do it 3 or 4 times a week.

At 6'/205 your joints are going to take a pounding, so you should be wearing a cushioned shoe, preferably with some structure. I'd recommend the Brooks Beast. It's a traditional road-running shoe designed for heavier folks--it'll save your joints quite a bit of stress. Also, Hoka makes some great shoes (although they look insane to most people). I'd highly recommend those too, but they retail very high, but can be found online for less than 100 bucks. Hokas are the "go-to" shoes for most ultra-runners, as they are designed to absorb most of the shock--which at your weight is what you're looking for. I can't remember the name of the Hoka road model...Stinson? Stinson Evo? Heck, they probably have a few road models--if you're training on roads, then any road Hoka should be excellent.

I trained/raced in New Balance exclusively for over a decade. They make good shoes BUT they also make a crap-ton of "fashion" shoes and they change their models incessantly. You really have to know which specific model you're buying with them as they have so many. Contrast that to Asics--you can just tell somebody to go out and buy Asics Kayano and you know they'll be wearing a solid running shoe. If you're fond of New Balance, that's great, but do some serious research on running websites as to which models are best. Personally, at your size, I'd be buying a pair of Brooks Beasts.

I'm glad you mentioned building endurance and not speed. Speed is a by-product of endurance, and it is smarter to focus on that. I'll be frank with you--you will not build any running endurance if you only do it once a week--it's impossible. There's a lot of ways to tackle it, however, and you can do it pretty easily. Here's the bottom line up front--once you get a decent baseline for jogging, you can do anything. By that I mean, once you're able to run X miles at a decent pace, you can EASILY tweak your training to get faster or go longer. Since you're just starting, I'd consider doing a jog 4 or 5 times a week. Pick a distance (not a time). Let's say it's 1 mile. For the first week, run a mile every day (M-F). Next week, push it to 1.5 miles. Don't concern yourself with the pace--the jogging motion is more important (don't walk). Go up gradually every week. Using this method you can easily go from not running to running 5 miles fairly quickly. In this building phase your real goal is to focus on your form and to just have the discipline to do it. Once you can run 5 miles daily without walking you're set. I know 5 miles can sound crazy--it is not. It is easy. By Thanksgiving you'll be able to run 5 miles in the time it might now take you to cover 2 miles.

I should note that the general rule of thumb with training is to not increase your distance more than 10% per week. Although this is a good rule, it does not apply at the extreme low-end of training (beginner). As long as you're not obese or have medical conditions, going from 1 mile to 1.5 miles is perfectly fine.
